specAnchors.text: know and use the relationship between weight, mass and gravitational field strength: weight = mass × gravitational field strength W = m × g

primer.text: Bathroom scales conflate two very different quantities. Mass counts the matter in you and never changes location; weight is the gravitational force on that matter and changes from planet to planet. This note separates the pair and builds the one-equation bridge between them.

modules.title: Weight, mass and gravitational fields
modules.opening: Weight is the force an object with mass experiences inside a gravitational field — nothing more, nothing less. Mass counts matter and is a scalar; weight is a force and is a vector. This lesson pins the definitions and explains why planets, not objects, decide the weight reading.
keyPoints: Weight is the force experienced by an object with mass when placed in a gravitational field.
Mass measures the amount of matter in an object; it is a scalar with magnitude only.
Weight is a force, and forces carry magnitude and direction, so weight is a vector.
Different planets have different gravitational field strengths; more massive planets pull more strongly.
An object's mass stays fixed from planet to planet, while its weight follows the local field.

low.restatement: Mass is how much matter you contain; weight is the pull a planet exerts on that matter.
low.analogy: Mass is the amount of luggage you pack; weight is how heavily the local gravity drags on the bags — repack nothing, change worlds, feel the difference.
low.examPointer: Call the force 'weight', never bare 'gravity' — examiners mark the loose word wrong.

medium.restatement: The scalar/vector split settles the vocabulary: mass reports a magnitude only; weight reports a magnitude and points towards the attracting body's centre.
medium.analogy: Mass is printed on the box; weight is the arrow the planet draws on it, always pointing down-hill in the local field.
medium.examPointer: Comparing Earth and Moon questions want both halves: same mass, different g, therefore different weight.

modules.title: Calculating weight with W = m × g
sourceHeadings: Weight, mass and gravitational field strength
modules.opening: One line of arithmetic joins the three ideas: W = m × g. The gravitational field strength g does the planet's work — about 10 N/kg on Earth, about 2 N/kg on the Moon — and the same g doubles as the freefall acceleration. This lesson works the equation in both directions.
keyPoints: The relationship is W = m × g: weight in newtons, mass in kilograms, gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram.
Earth's gravitational field strength is 10 N/kg.
The same g describes the acceleration of freefall in a gravitational field, 10 m/s² on Earth.
Mass and weight are directly proportional: double one and the other doubles.
The Moon's field is about 2 N/kg, so the same mass weighs about five times less there.

low.restatement: Multiply the mass by the local field strength and you have the weight: W = m × g.
low.analogy: g is an exchange rate between kilograms and newtons — Earth converts at 10, the Moon at 2.
low.examPointer: g's value is given in exams; the skill is substituting it correctly, not memorising it.

medium.restatement: The proportionality is the working law: weight tracks mass linearly for a fixed field, and tracks the field linearly for a fixed mass — the two moves every rearranged question uses.
medium.analogy: A radio volume knob with two sliders: slide the mass or slide the field, and the weight output moves in exact proportion.
medium.examPointer: Quote g's two faces when asked — 10 N/kg as a field strength, 10 m/s² as a freefall acceleration; they are one quantity seen two ways.

glossary.definition: The force experienced by an object with mass when placed in a gravitational field.
A measure of the amount of matter in an object; a scalar.
The force per unit mass exerted by a gravitational field, in newtons per kilogram.
Motion under gravity alone; its acceleration equals g.

workedExample.prompt: Isabelle has a mass of 40 kg. Earth's gravitational field strength is 10 N/kg and the Moon's is 2 N/kg. Discuss the difference between her weight on Earth and on the Moon.
steps: State the equation linking weight and mass: W = m × g.
List the known values: m = 40 kg, Earth g = 10 N/kg, Moon g = 2 N/kg.
Compare: Earth's larger field strength gives the larger weight — five times larger for the same mass.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Isabelle weighs 400 N on Earth and 80 N on the Moon; her mass is 40 kg in both places.
